# Vizney Blocks

> Charts you read through their motion and the dashboard controls that go with them, as copy-paste HTML cards: 5 charts and 5 controls (v0.74). One card is an HTML snippet that bundles <style>, a JSON data block and <script>; paste it inside <body> and it draws itself. Change only the values in the card's <script type="application/json">. © 2026 Vizney · MIT License.

How to use:
- Pick a card by what it shows (the first sentences of each card below). The cards on this page are all there are; when none fits, draw that part yourself and say so, rather than bending a card. Card names describe the shape, not the metric, so put what the values are in the JSON title.
- Paste the card code from the links (.txt) below as it is and change only the JSON values. Do not edit the styles or the script. To use the same card several times, paste the whole card code again and change each JSON.
- A card fills the width of its slot. A chart card is 1, 1.5 or 2 units tall (1 unit = 168px, --vzb-unit), and every chart card is now 2 units (336px). The controls (Date Picker · Range Slider · Filter Chips · Select Menu · Download Button) draw only the control, with no card head or frame, at the height of the control itself. Their background is left empty, so set "theme" to match where they sit ("dark" on a dark background).
- For several cards, give the wrapper a grid: display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 340px), 1fr)); gap:16px. Keep a chart card at least 340px wide. A chart that reads along a long axis (13 months of bars, the 20 cells across a waffle, rank lines) reads better with two columns or the full width. Put the controls as they are in a filter bar above the charts or in the page header.
- Change colors and the font with the --vzb-* variables on :root (--vzb-primary, --vzb-font, …). The variable list and what each one does are in https://blocks.vizney.com/tokens.css (the same content as the :where(:root) block in the card code). The background is picked per card with "theme" in its JSON: empty is white with blue as the first data color, "dark" is Vizney black with yellow as the first data color.
- The motion has roles, and each role has one value in the same variable list. Things you touch: --vzb-follow (held by the pointer, no overshoot), --vzb-settle (let go, opened or widened: one small overshoot), --vzb-pop (a released button, a picked item, a surfacing label: a clear bounce), --vzb-fade and --vzb-press (times). Things that carry a value: --vzb-move, which never overshoots, because a height or a position is the value and a bounce would show a wrong value for a moment. Rhythm: --vzb-lead (the wait before a card starts), --vzb-seq (the time items share out when they move in turn) and --vzb-rest (the pause before a loop). A spring is written 'stiffness damping'; for CSS transitions use the ready-made time and curve, such as transition: transform var(--vzb-pop-t) var(--vzb-pop-e). When you add elements of your own around the cards (KPI tiles, tables, tabs), move them with the same variables and keep the rule: a value never bounces.
- Common fields: title (what the values are), subtitle (the period and the basis), format (usd dollar amounts, shortened to $745.6K · $1.2M · count a count, with its unit in unit · pct a percentage (3.4 is 3.4%), changes in pp · days a number of days · eok and krw are Korean won notations), decimals (decimal places; empty lets the card decide), better (up · down · neutral), labels (period names, the same length as the values; null for a period without a value), lang (en: the words the card prints itself in English), theme. Controls: label (the name screen readers read; not drawn on screen) and name (detail.name of the control's events). Each card's own fields are in the example JSON of its code and in its rules below.
- The amount over a limit, shares, ranks, changes and totals are computed by the card, so do not write them in the JSON. Give amounts as raw values, not rounded or divided into thousands or millions.
- A chart card plays once when it comes into view and stops on its last frame. The still frame reads correctly by itself. The motion carries the data, so cards play whatever the reduced-motion setting of the system; mouse-over and keyboard focus pause them, and a replay button or player sits on the card. A wrapper with data-vzb-loop makes the card repeat; a card that keeps moving makes its neighbours hard to read, so use that only on a showcase such as a gallery.
- A card is a snippet pasted into the HTML document as it is. Inserted with innerHTML or React's dangerouslySetInnerHTML, the card's <script> does not run.
- Coding agents can install the skill (the same cards and rules): npx skills add yehwanhwang/vizney-blocks
- Gallery: https://blocks.vizney.com/ · Korean: https://blocks.vizney.com/ko/ (llms.txt: https://blocks.vizney.com/ko/llms.txt) · Source: https://github.com/yehwanhwang/vizney-blocks

## Charts

Each chart card belongs to a chart type of the Vizney chart guide (https://www.vizney.com/chart-guide/); its motion is what the data means, not decoration.

- [Bar Overflow](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/bar-overflow.txt) · Bar Chart (https://www.vizney.com/bar-chart-in-tableau/): Bars for each period stand against one horizontal line, the same limit for every period, and only the parts above the line blink red. Use it for a trend with the same limit each period, such as a monthly budget or a monthly capacity. Do not use it for a target, where more is better. Rules: Write the periods in labels, their values in values (the same length) and one limit for every period in limit. Write null for a period with no value: its slot stays empty, since leaving the period out would shift the time axis. The name of the line (limitLabel, Limit when empty) and its value always sit at the right end of the line, outside the bars (the name above the line, the value below), because a label placed in a gap between bars moves with the data and is hard to find. One horizontal line means you only compare bar tops with the line to see which periods went over. Below the line the bars are gray; only the part above it is red. The card writes the excess above each bar that went over (left out when the slot is too narrow), and pointing at a bar does not hide it, because a number that vanishes under the pointer looks like an error; the tooltip does not repeat that excess but gives the value, the limit and the share of the limit (for a bar whose excess label was left out, the tooltip adds the excess). On the line below, the card writes how many periods went over and the total excess. Keeping color for the excess makes what needs attention come first. For a rate (pct) the total is left out. Use it only for limits that should not be crossed. On a target where more is better, the periods that met it would blink red like a warning. If each period has a different limit, one line cannot compare them, so do not use this card. When the card comes into view the line is already drawn, the bars rise one by one from the left, then only the parts above the line blink three times and stop. No bar is drawn before it rises. The still frame alone shows which periods went over and by how much. Replay it with the button at the top right. When the data changes and the card redraws, it does not play from the start: the bars on screen move to the new values (a period with the same name is the same bar, a new period grows from the baseline and a removed one fades out), because a chart swapped at once does not show what changed or by how much. When the scale changes, values and scale move one after the other so that no bar grows while its value falls, and only the bars that newly crossed the limit blink once. A monthly trend shows 13 months.
- [Waffle Flip](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/waffle-flip.txt) · Waffle Chart (https://www.vizney.com/waffle-chart-in-tableau/): A card that draws shares as a 100-cell waffle and flips, one by one, the cells that changed hands since the earlier period. Use it to show how much one item's share grew or shrank, such as a market share or a sales mix. It draws the change between two periods only. Rules: List 2 to 4 items in items, each with the raw values (units sold, sales and so on) of the periods (the earlier one, then the later one) in values. The card computes the shares and the change in points. Each period's cells add up to 100 by giving the leftover cells to the largest remainders (one cell is 1%). With a single period in periods, the card draws that period's cells with no period switch. When filtering leaves no item, give an empty items array for an empty card. Name the item to point at in focus (empty means the first item). Only that item takes the first data color; the others are gray steps, from dark to light in the order listed. With color on one item only, the cells it gained or lost stand out first. There are three gray steps, so with five items or more, fold the small ones into Others. Cells fill from the top left, column by column, starting with the focus item (a column of 5 cells is 5%). So when its share grows or shrinks, the cells flip at the end of its block, and a bracket under them gives the change in points. The big number is the focus item's share, and the badge color follows better (up · down). The cells sit right under the big number and grow as large as the space left within the 2-unit height and the width allows. With an inner width of 520px or more, the legend stands in a column to the right of the cells; narrower, it goes below them. With 20 cells across, a wider slot means larger cells, so the flips are easier to see. With two periods, a period switch sits at the top right of the head. When the card comes into view, the earlier period's cells sit still, then the switch moves to the later period and only the changed cells flip one after another, while the big number and the legend shares follow the visible cells one point at a time. When all have flipped, the bracket and the badge appear and the card stops. The still frame alone shows the current share and how far it moved. Click the switch or use the left and right arrow keys to go back and forth between the two periods (going back, the cells flip in reverse, last flipped first); the switch tells which period the big number and the legend show, so the earlier values are always one step away. When the data changes and the card redraws, it draws the picked period's still frame at once. Hover a cell, or focus the chart and press the left and right arrow keys, to see that item's share (one decimal) and raw value for the period on screen, plus the change in points against the earlier period when the later one is on screen.
- [Bump Race](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/bump-race.txt) · Bump Chart (https://www.vizney.com/bump-chart-in-tableau/): A card that ranks the items in every period, joins the ranks with S-curves, and plays through the periods one at a time so the moments the order changes are visible. Use it to show how products, channels or branches moved up and down over a year, above all how far one item climbed. Ranks hide the size of the differences, so when the gaps matter, use a line chart. Rules: Put the period names in labels and 2 to 8 items in items, each with the value of every period (units sold and so on) in values. The card ranks each period from the largest value (better: down makes the smallest value rank 1). Ties follow the previous period's rank, then the listed order, and a null value takes the item out of that period's ranking and breaks its line. Draw 13 months for a monthly trend. Name the item to follow in focus (empty means the first item). Only that item takes the first data color; the rest stay gray, so one path can be followed while the others cross. The label at the end of each line gives the current rank and the name, in place of a legend. Click a line or a label (on the keyboard, pick it with the up and down arrow keys and press Enter) to make that item the one in color, so any item's path can be followed the same way. Rank 1 is at the top and periods are joined with S-curves. Labels ride on the right of the line ends and move with them, so the chart keeps room on the right for the longest label. The scrubber at the bottom is the time axis, so there is no separate period axis: the current period sits under its thumb, with the first and last periods at its ends. When the card comes into view it waits on the first period, then moves on about every half second while the lines grow and the labels move up and down to that period's ranks, so each overtake is visible. It stops on the last period, and the still frame reads as an ordinary bump chart. Rewind, play/pause and fast-forward buttons sit to the right of the scrubber, under the label column. Play starts where the card stopped (from the start when at the end); rewind and fast-forward move one period per click, or keep moving at three times the playing speed while held and stop on the nearest period on release. Drag or click the scrubber, or press the left and right arrow keys, to move one period at a time. When the data changes and the card redraws, it draws the picked period at once. Hover a line, or focus the chart and press the up and down arrow keys, to see that period's rank, value and move against the previous period while the other items fade. Playback pauses while the pointer is over the chart or the chart has keyboard focus.
- [Waterfall Walk](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/waterfall-walk.txt) · Waterfall Chart (https://www.vizney.com/waterfall-chart-in-tableau/): A card that joins what raised and what cut a value between a starting point and an end point, as one bar per item. On play, dots appear one by one from the level where the last bar ended and walk to the next item, the bar then rises or falls from that level, and the name and value attached to its end travel with it. Use it to tell, in order, what moved a value between two points: how the members at the start of the year became the members at the end through sign-ups and cancellations, which drivers turned last year's operating profit into this year's, or how much of revenue is left as operating profit and net income after costs. Do not use it for a trend over periods. Rules: List the items in items in reading order. The first item is the starting value ({ "name": "Jan 1", "value": 720 }), and each change is an item whose value is + for an increase and - for a decrease. Where the end value should stand, put { "name": "Dec 31", "total": true } and leave its value out: the card computes totals so that the items and the totals never disagree. A total item in the middle stands the running total there as a subtotal (like operating profit on an income statement). The card keeps your order, so list the items in the order you explain them (for example the increases, then the decreases). Three to seven changes read well; with more, group the small ones as Other. An item whose value is null keeps its slot and passes the level on unchanged, and when the filter leaves no item, give items as an empty array to draw an empty state. Total bars (the first item and every total item) stand on the floor (0) in gray, and each change bar starts at the level where the bar before it ended and moves up or down by its amount. A dotted line carries that level from bar to bar, so the eye can follow where the next bar starts; the dots fill the space between two bars at even intervals. Changes that raise the result are green and those that lower it are red; set better to down for a measure where lower is better, or to neutral to draw every change in the first data color. Keeping color for good and bad shows first what lifted and what cut the result. So that color is never the only cue, change values always carry a + or - sign, and the text sits above a bar that raises the level and below one that lowers it. Names and values are printed together just outside the end each bar arrives at, not under the axis, so you can read what changed and by how much right where you are looking. Keep names short, because they sit at the bar ends (long ones are shortened). Where a slot is too narrow and the text would overlap a neighbor's text or bar, it is nudged sideways or moved further from the bar, and if there is still no room, the name and then the value are left out (the tooltip and the table keep them). Pointing at a bar does not hide its name, value or callout; the tooltip does not repeat that value but tells how it came about (for a change, where the running total moved from and to; for a total, 'first item → this total'), because a number that vanishes under the pointer looks like an error. There is no large figure under the title: a callout rising from the end bar (the last total item) gives its name, the end value, and the change against the first item (a difference instead of a percentage when the start is 0 or below). Writing the number once and giving that height to the chart makes the differences in bar height easier to see. For a flow that shows how much of the first item is left, like an income statement, set compare to share to print its share of the first item instead. Values below 0 are drawn under the floor line. When the card comes into view, the first bar is already in place, and then the items move one at a time from the left. Dots appear one by one from the level where the last bar ended and walk to the next slot, and the bar rises or falls from that level with its name and value riding on its end. The value counts what is drawn so far (from +0 up to +360). At a total, the level reached pours down into a bar until it meets the floor, and when the end bar is full, the callout pops out of it and the card stops. The motion takes one step at a time in that order because it is what a waterfall chart says: each step starts where the one before it ended. The still frame reads as an ordinary waterfall chart. The replay button at the top right plays it again, and when the data changes and the card redraws, it draws the last frame at once. Hover a bar, or focus the chart and press the left and right arrows, to see a change with its running total (before → after), or a total with its change against the first item (its share of the first item when compare is share), with only that bar left at full strength. Playback pauses while the pointer is over the chart or the keyboard focus is on it.
- [Funnel Wave](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/funnel-wave.txt) · Funnel Chart (https://www.vizney.com/funnel-chart-in-tableau/): A card for stages passed in a fixed order, like lead to won deal, that shows how much of the first stage is still left at each stage on the way to the end, counting the first stage as 100. Each stage is drawn as a water level for how many reached it, and on play the water flows in from the left, drops to the level of what is left at each boundary and runs to the end. Use it for sales stages, purchase conversion or sign-up steps when you report the share left of the start and the overall conversion. Do not use it to compare items that have no order. Rules: Write the stages in items in order ({ "name": "Leads", "value": 2400 }). A value is how many reached that stage; the card computes the share of the first stage, each stage's conversion rate (the share that moved on from the previous stage) and the overall conversion (from the first stage to the last), so do not write them. Three to six stages read well. When the filter leaves no stage, give items as an empty array to draw an empty state. The stages sit side by side as cells of the same width, and the water in each cell stands at its share of the first stage. Heights are measured from the floor, so cells compare directly. A pill on the water in each cell gives that share (100% → 55% → 26% → 17% → 11%), so how much of the first 100 is left reads first, and the pill of the last stage is the conversion from the first stage to the last. A funnel is usually read as how much of the start made it to the end, so this share comes first, and the share that moved on from the previous stage (the stage conversion rate) goes in the tooltip and the table. At each boundary the water runs down in an S curve to the level of the next stage, and a 2px divider in the card background color cuts the water and its surface line so the stages part clearly. The water is one flow, so it is painted in the first color only, with each stage mixed into white by a different amount so the cells part by tone. The first stage is the lightest and the last the deepest, so the part that made it to the end shows first. On a dark background it is also mixed into white, so the yellow never turns muddy. Under each cell are the stage value and name. Names are shortened to fit the cell, so keep them short (the tooltip and the table keep them whole). When the cells are narrow, the text steps down one size. When it comes into view, the water flows in from the left, drops to the level of what is left at each boundary, runs to the right end, laps lightly against the end wall and settles. The value of each stage the water reaches counts up from 0, and the pill of a cell rises when the water passes its middle. The waves always die down and stop, so the water levels in the still frame are the values. The replay button at the top right plays it again. When the data changes and the card redraws, the water does not flow in from the start: in each cell it moves from where it stands to the new level without overshooting, because a chart swapped at once does not show which stage changed or by how much. The pill rides the water up and down, and the share on the pill and the value under the cell follow the water on screen. While the water in a cell is moving, the back layers rise a few pixels above it to show which cells are changing, and the front water is always at the value. A stage with the same name in the same place is the same stage; when the number of stages changes, the card draws its last frame at once. Hover a stage, or focus the chart and press the left and right arrows, and the water in that cell ripples gently in three overlapping layers and settles in about two seconds (the two back layers are lighter versions of the same tone). The water level is the value, so the ripples stay within a few pixels and never get in the way of reading the height. The pill of that cell does not hide: it fills with the first color and grows a little, because a number that vanishes under the pointer looks like an error. The tooltip sits beside the pill and does not repeat its share; it gives the values the share is made of ('first stage value → this stage value', with an arrow for the order) and the share that moved on from the previous stage. Moving the mouse raises waves as if your hand pushed the water, and they die down. Hovering with the mouse or focusing with the keyboard pauses the flow. Screen readers get a table of stage, value, share from the previous stage and share of the first stage.

## Controls

Controls set the period, the ranges and the items of a screen, and download its data. They draw only the control, with no card head or frame, so you can put them anywhere, such as a filter bar above the charts or a page header. They fill the width of their slot and are as tall as the control itself. Their background is left empty, so pick theme to match the background they sit on (dark on a dark one), and write the name screen readers read in label. When the value changes, the card sends a vzb-change event (detail: { name, value }), and the current value is also written on the card as data-vzb-value. Listen for the event and change the text of the JSON inside a chart card, and that card draws again with the new data. The selected span and the thumbs are drawn in the text color so they do not compete with the data colors of the charts.

- [Date Picker](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/date-picker.txt): A control that picks a period (a start and an end date), or a single date, on a calendar. Use it to filter a screen by a date, such as the order date or a reference date. At rest it is one button with the current period and its number of days; press it and fields to type the dates and a month calendar rise below it. Rules: Write the starting period in value as YYYY-MM-DD, like ["2026-10-01", "2026-10-31"] (empty means the 30 days up to the reference date). Write the first and last dates with data in min and max: the dates outside are dimmed and cannot be picked, so no one picks a period without data. "today" in place of a date is the viewer's today: for a screen of data up to today, set "max": "today" and leave value empty, and it opens on the 30 days up to today every time. The reference date is max, or today when it is empty. For a parameter that is a single date, set "mode": "day" and write one date in value. List quick picks in presets to show them as chips under the calendar: last7 (last 7 days) · last30 (last 30 days) · month (this month) · lastmonth (last month) · quarter (this quarter) · year (this year) · all (min to max). All count from the reference date, and the chip that matches the current period is filled in the text color, so you can see which period is applied. About three chips fit on one line; more scroll sideways. Press two dates in turn to make a period. After the first one, a pale band and the number of days follow the pointer or the focus to the date it reaches, so you know the length while you pick. On the second date the band draws from the start to the end, the button switches to the new period, the number of days rolls, and the calendar closes. The fields at the top of the calendar take the start and end dates typed in (2026-10-01, 2026.10.1, 20261001 or 10/1/2026 all read; a date that cannot be read or picked turns its field red and is not applied), so no one has to click their way to a distant date. Press the month title for the twelve months, and again for twelve years, to jump to a distant month or year. The calendar draws five weeks (a month that spans six weeks fits six into the same height, so every month is as tall), and moving to another month slides it in the direction of time. Each change sends a vzb-change event. detail.name is name and detail.value is ["start", "end"] (the end date included; a single date when mode is day). The current value is also in the card's data-vzb-value. The button and the calendar always share one width (300px, or the slot when it is narrower), so the button does not grow or shrink as the period changes. When the period does not fit on the button, a period in the year of the reference date drops the year, and a longer one turns into numeric dates (10/17/26). The calendar floats over the content beside it instead of pushing it away, and opens upward when there is no room below. Set "align": "end" to push the button to the right end of the screen. Everything works from the keyboard: on the button, Enter, Space or the down arrow opens the calendar; in the calendar, the arrows move a day or a week, Page Up/Down a month (a year with Shift), Home/End to the start or end of the week, Enter or Space picks, and Esc closes. In the fields, Enter applies and closes. On the months and years, the arrows move, Enter picks and Esc goes back one level. The button, the band and its ends are drawn in the text color so they do not compete with the data colors of the charts.
- [Range Slider](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/range-slider.txt): A control that picks a numeric range with two thumbs. Use it to filter a screen by a continuous value such as order value or quantity. Give it the distribution of the values and, while you drag, bars rise over the rail to show how much data falls in the range. Rules: Drag or use the arrow keys to pick between min and max in steps of step (empty splits the range into about 100 steps). Give the first range in value as [start, end]; empty is the whole range. The picked values sit under the thumbs and move with them, by format; when they meet, they merge into one 'start – end'. Press a value (or Enter on a thumb) and start and end fields open in its place to type the values: a typed value is used as it is, not snapped to step (commas and units are ignored, and 1.2K or 60k read too), because filtering by an exact amount is common and hard to hit by dragging. Enter or leaving the fields applies; Esc cancels. Give counts, the number of records in each equal-width bin from min to max, and while you drag or move a thumb with the keys, a distribution panel rises over the rail: the bars inside the range take the text color and the count inside the range is written with noun (rows when empty). Picking by the range alone hides where the data piles up, which makes it easy to filter it away; at rest only the rail and the values remain, so the slider takes little room in a filter bar. A value inside a bin is counted for the share of the bin it covers, so step can be finer than the bin width. Each time the value changes, the card sends a vzb-change event. detail.name is name and detail.value is [start, end] as numbers. The current value is also on the card as data-vzb-value. Drag a thumb, press the rail to bring the nearer thumb there, or focus a thumb and press the arrow keys to move one step (Page Up and Down about ten steps, Home and End to the end). The thumbs follow like a spring; bars rise a little as they enter the range, nearest to the moving thumb first, and dip as they leave.
- [Filter Chips](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/filter-chips.txt): A control that picks several items from a fixed list as chips. Use it to filter a screen by a few names, such as channels or regions. The All chip at the front shows how many are picked. Rules: List the items in options and the first picks in value (empty picks all). Past three rows the chips go on one row that scrolls sideways, so about 8 items, all visible at a glance, fit best. The All chip at the front (all; empty means "All", an empty string leaves it out) shows the number picked as a rolling number, and pressing it picks everything, or clears everything when all are picked. How many are on is always in view, so a filter is never left on by mistake. Each time the value changes, the card sends a vzb-change event. detail.name is name and detail.value is the picked items in the order of options. The current value is also on the card as data-vzb-value. A chip squashes a little when pressed and springs back, and when picked a check is drawn as the chip widens. Picked chips are filled with the text color so they do not compete with the data colors of the charts. Tab moves between chips and Space or Enter picks.
- [Select Menu](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/select-menu.txt): A control that opens a list to search and pick from when there are too many items to lay out as chips. Use it for filters with dozens of names, such as countries, regions, stores or products. At rest it is one button with what is picked; press it and a search field and the list rise below it. With about eight items, Filter Chips, which show everything at a glance, are the better fit. Rules: List the items in options as names or as { "name": "Germany", "count": 1740 }, and the first picks in value (empty picks all). With count, each row shows how much data the item holds as a small bar (against the largest item) and a number, and the bars grow from zero as the list opens. You see where the data sits before you pick, so you are less likely to pick only items with almost no data and get an empty chart. noun is the word screen readers read after the number. The button reads all (All when empty) when everything is picked, 'None picked' when nothing is, and otherwise the picked names in options order, shortened to '+the rest' when they do not fit. The badge on the right rolls to the number picked, so you never forget a filter is on. For a parameter that takes one item, set "mode": "one" and write one name in value: there is no badge or select-all row, and picking closes the list. Typing in the search field keeps only the matching items (the rest fold away), and the matching letters turn bold with an underline that draws in. Case does not matter, and Korean names also match by initial consonants (ㄱ finds 경기, 강원, 경남…). A long list is hard to scan by eye. Select all and Clear act on the matches while you search. The list shows up to six rows and scrolls inside for more. Each change sends a vzb-change event. detail.name is name and detail.value is the picked items in options order (one name when mode is one). The current value is also in the card's data-vzb-value. The button and the list always share one width (300px, or the slot when it is narrower); the list floats over the content beside it instead of pushing it away, and opens upward when there is no room below. Set "align": "end" at the right end of the screen. Everything works from the keyboard. Enter, Space or the down arrow on the button opens the list with the focus in the search field; the up and down arrows (Page Up/Down for five rows) move between items and Enter picks. Esc clears the search, or closes the list when the search is empty. A picked row fills its box in the text color and draws a check, so it does not compete with the data colors of the charts.
- [Download Button](https://blocks.vizney.com/cards/download-button.txt): A button that downloads the data of a chart card on the screen as a file. It starts as an icon alone; hover and the formats to pick from (CSV, JSON, PNG) come out. Use it to export exactly what the controls show. Rules: Write the kind of the card to download in target (its data-vzb, e.g. bar-overflow). The table comes from the current JSON of the first such card on the page: items, else labels with values (adding limit and target as columns when present), labels with series, else the first array of objects. It reads the JSON after the controls changed it, so you get what you see. List the formats in formats (csv, json, png; empty means all three). The CSV starts with a BOM so Excel reads non-English text correctly, and the PNG is the card as you see it at twice the size (its text may be drawn in a font installed on the device). The file name is filename plus the extension of the format. An icon alone takes little room on the screen; hover it, reach it with the keyboard or press it and the button widens and the formats come out one by one. Pressing the icon again while open downloads the first format, Esc closes it, and the left and right arrows move between the formats. The widened button floats over what is next to it instead of pushing it, and when there is no room on the right it opens to the left, keeping the icon in place. To put it at the right end, as at the top right of a screen, set align to end: the icon sits at the right end and the button opens to the left. Before downloading, the card sends a vzb-download event (detail: { name, target, format, filename, rows }). If the page calls preventDefault() the card makes no file, so a screen that fetches the source data from a server can use the same button. When the file is saved, the arrow drops into the tray and turns into a check, and the format and the number of rows (for a PNG, its size) roll up next to the button and fade after 1.8 s. When there is nothing to download, the button shakes and says "No data".

## Connecting controls and charts

Controls and charts do not know each other. A short page script takes a control's event and rewrites the chart card's JSON.

- A control sends a vzb-change event from its card whenever its value changes (it bubbles, so listen on document). detail is { name, value }, where name is the name in that control's JSON. Date Picker's value is ["start", "end"] as date strings (YYYY-MM-DD, the end date included); Range Slider's value is [from, to] as numbers; Filter Chips' value is the picked items in the order of options. The current value is also on the card, as JSON in its data-vzb-value attribute.
- A control sends nothing when it first draws. Write the control's value and the chart's JSON for the same starting condition.
- A chart card redraws by itself when the text of its <script type="application/json"> changes. The page keeps the full data; on an event it filters the data, builds the chart's JSON from the result and writes it back. The redrawn card does not play from the start, and it keeps the period and the item the viewer picked. Bar Overflow moves the bars on screen from where they are to the new values; a period with the same name is the same bar, so keep the names in labels unchanged when you filter. Funnel Wave moves the water in each cell from where it stands to the new level, and the share on the pill and the value under the cell follow the water; a stage with the same name in the same place is the same stage, so keep the stages and their order in items and change only the values (when the number of stages changes, it draws at once). The other chart cards draw their last frame at once.
- When the filter leaves nothing, give an empty array. Bar Overflow draws an empty state for "labels": [], and Waffle Flip, Bump Race, Waterfall Walk and Funnel Wave for "items": [], instead of an error.
- With two cards of the same kind on a page, wrap each in an element with an id and address it through that id (#spend in the example).
- Download Button downloads the current JSON of the first card on the page whose data-vzb is its target, so the file holds what the controls left on screen. Before that it sends a vzb-download event (detail: { name, target, format, filename, rows }); if the page calls preventDefault(), the card makes no file, so a screen that gets the source data from a server can use the same button.

```html
<div><!-- the Filter Chips card code, with "name": "channel" --></div>
<div id="spend"><!-- the Bar Overflow card code --></div>
<script>
// The full data the page holds: the period names and the monthly values of each channel.
const LABELS = ["Nov '25", "Dec '25", "Jan '26"];
const SPEND = { Social: [8600, 16200, 9700], Search: [9500, 10300, 10100] };
document.addEventListener('vzb-change', (e) => {
  if (e.detail.name !== 'channel') return;
  const picked = e.detail.value;   // the channels picked
  const src = document.querySelector('#spend .vzb-card script[type="application/json"]');
  const d = JSON.parse(src.textContent);
  d.labels = picked.length ? LABELS : [];   // nothing picked: an empty array, and the card draws its empty state
  d.values = d.labels.map((_, t) => picked.reduce((sum, c) => sum + SPEND[c][t], 0));
  src.textContent = JSON.stringify(d);   // the card redraws when this text changes
});
</script>
```
